title: Trump Just Cut Tariffs on India to 18 Per Cent. Here Is What Every NRI Needs to Know Before the July 9 Deadline.
excerpt: The first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement is taking shape. India is pushing for full exemption from the 26 per cent reciprocal tariff while protecting agriculture and dairy. The clock runs out in four weeks.
body:
After months of tariff escalation that saw duties on Indian goods spike as high as 50 per cent, the contours of a deal are emerging. The Trump administration has signalled a reduction in tariffs on India to 18 per cent — a significant step down from the 26 per cent reciprocal tariff announced in April and the punitive 50 per cent levy imposed briefly over India's Russian oil purchases. Both sides are now racing to finalise the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement before the 90-day tariff pause expires on July 9.

## What Is on the Table

The agreement in progress — dubbed "Mission 500" by both governments — aims to more than double bilateral trade between India and the US to $500 billion by 2030. The first tranche focuses on goods, non-tariff barriers, and some service sectors, including digital services.

India is pushing for full exemption from the 26 per cent additional tariff and the removal of the 10 per cent baseline tariff that currently applies to all Indian exports. In return, Washington wants duty concessions on industrial goods, electric vehicles, wines, petrochemical products, dairy, and agricultural items including apples, tree nuts, and genetically modified crops.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, who met with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in Washington last week, said both sides were moving "swiftly" toward finalising the first tranche, possibly by mid-July. "Talks are moving positively," Goyal said. "We are trying that the 26 per cent additional duty and the 10 per cent baseline tariff should not be there for India."

India has drawn clear red lines. GM crop imports remain a non-starter due to Indian regulatory norms, though New Delhi is open to importing non-GM products like alfalfa hay for cattle feed. Agriculture and dairy remain sensitive sectors where India may impose quotas or minimum import prices rather than open market access.

## The Surplus Capacity Dispute

A separate front has opened. The US Trade Representative is considering an additional tariff on India, alleging excess capacity in textiles and other sectors that it claims is hurting American industry. India has rejected the charge. Commerce Secretary Sunil Barthwal told Reuters that India's exports are driven by genuine demand, not subsidised overproduction.

The USTR has also proposed a 12.5 per cent additional tariff on imports from India and other countries, citing alleged use of forced labour. India has said these levies are not final as negotiations under the Section 301 process continue.

"The move appears aimed at a particular country while also serving other trade-related aims," Barthwal said — a diplomatic way of suggesting the tariff threat is leverage, not policy.

## The Gold Complication

Separately, India's decision to raise gold import duties has created an unintended feedback loop. Gold smuggling, which had fallen from 156 metric tons in 2023 to just 20.4 tons in 2025 after a duty cut, is surging again. Grey-market discounts have pushed domestic legal gold prices down by more than $100 an ounce, making legitimate refining uneconomical and disrupting the entire supply chain.

India imported 45.6 tons of gold in April, but legal imports may have halved in May as banks and refiners scaled back. For NRIs who buy gold during visits home — still a significant cultural and financial practice — the price gap between legal and grey-market gold is now wide enough to matter.

## What NRIs Should Watch

**Remittance impact.** If the deal holds at 18 per cent and the baseline tariff is removed, Indian export sectors that employ millions — textiles, gems, leather, shrimp, chemicals — will get breathing room. That strengthens the rupee and reduces pressure on remittance-dependent families.

**IT services carve-out.** Digital services are explicitly on the table. Any concessions here could affect H-1B-heavy sectors and the broader US-India tech corridor. NRIs working in tech should watch whether the deal includes provisions on data localisation, cross-border digital payments, or service-sector market access.

**Agricultural politics.** India's refusal to open its agricultural market to GM crops and American dairy will be framed in the US as protectionism. But for Indian consumers — and for NRIs who care about what India's food system looks like — it is a line in the sand that has both scientific and cultural dimensions.

**The July 9 cliff.** If no deal is reached by then, the 26 per cent reciprocal tariff snaps back. Markets will price this in well before the deadline. For NRIs with portfolios spanning both countries, the next four weeks are a hedging window, not a waiting period.

## The Bigger Picture

India is not negotiating in isolation. It has simultaneously finalised a landmark trade deal with the European Union — an agreement that represents a quarter of the world's economy and took nearly two decades to close. "People around the world are calling this the mother of all deals," Prime Minister Modi said of the India-EU pact.

The strategy is clear: diversify trade relationships so that no single bilateral friction — even with the world's largest economy — can derail India's growth trajectory. For the eight million NRIs in America, this is a bet worth understanding. The country you left is no longer negotiating from weakness. The question is whether the country you live in recognises that.
